issues.legal_issue: A class-wide exemption of buildings owned by cooperative societies from rent-control protections is consistent with equality when the societies’ regulated structure and the circumstances supporting the exemption provide a rational connection to the purposes of rent control.
material_facts: The petitioners were tenants in buildings owned by a cooperative society and challenged a notification exempting buildings owned by all cooperative societies from the rent-control statute.
Cooperative societies were established to promote members’ economic interests through cooperative principles and to advance social and economic welfare.
The governing cooperative legislation restricted distributions of profits through limits on dividends and bonuses and required allocations to various funds.

The State asserted that cooperative societies did not ordinarily purchase buildings as a business for letting them out, that societies had faced hardship under the rent-control law, and that withdrawing tenant protections would not lead to rack-renting or unreasonable eviction.
The State’s factual assertions were unchallenged; the court also noted the hardship experienced by the society whose buildings the tenants occupied.
issues.conclusion: The exemption notification was a valid exercise of the statutory exemption power and did not violate the constitutional guarantee of equality; the petitions were dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 29 of the Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960, the exemption power must be exercised consistently with the guidance of that Act’s purpose and provisions. Article 14 permits a classification where the differentia has a rational nexus to the object of the law. Sections 4 and 62 of the Tamil Nadu Co-operative Societies Act, 1961, and rule 46 of the rules made under it reflect cooperative principles and restrict the distribution of profits, distinguishing cooperative societies from commercial landlords and supporting an inference that they would not engage in rack-renting or unreasonable eviction. The State’s unchallenged evidence of cooperative societies’ welfare activities, operational difficulties, and lack of a letting business further supported the nexus. Baburao Shantaram More v. Bombay Housing Board did not establish that exemptions for cooperative-owned buildings are invalid; it concerned a different exemption and did not decide that question.

rule.if: challenge_to_class_wide_rent_control_exemption and cooperative_society_owned_buildings and regulated_distribution_of_cooperative_profits and cooperative_welfare_purpose and no_building_letting_business and state_found_no_expected_rack_renting_or_unreasonable_eviction and unchallenged_evidence_of_operational_hardship

predicates.challenge_to_class_wide_rent_control_exe: A party brings a constitutional challenge to an exemption from rent-control protections that applies to a class of property owners.
predicates.cooperative_society_owned_buildings: The exempted buildings are owned by cooperative societies.
predicates.regulated_distribution_of_cooperative_pr: The legal framework governing the owners restricts distributions of profits and requires some profits to be allocated to designated funds.
predicates.cooperative_welfare_purpose: The owners operate on cooperative principles to promote members’ economic interests and broader social or economic welfare.
predicates.no_building_letting_business: The owners do not conduct the purchase of buildings for the purpose of letting them out as a business.
predicates.state_found_no_expected_rack_renting_or_: The government determined that removing rent-control protections for the class was not expected to result in rack-renting or unreasonable eviction.
predicates.unchallenged_evidence_of_operational_har: The government presented evidence that applying rent-control restrictions caused operational hardship to members of the class, and that evidence was not challenged.

issues.definition: When a class-wide rent-control exemption is challenged and the exempted cooperative owners have regulated profit distributions, a welfare purpose, no building-letting business, and unchallenged support for the government’s conclusion that the exemption will not produce the targeted abuses but will relieve operational hardship, the exemption is constitutionally valid.
